client: I've been really struggling since I failed my calculus final last month. It's like this constant voice in my head telling me I'm not smart enough for my major, that I somehow fooled everyone into thinking I belonged here. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day, the grade is still there and I still don't know if I can actually do this.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling shaken — a difficult grade can hit hard, especially when it feels like it says something bigger about who you are and whether you belong. That voice telling you you're a fraud is incredibly common among capable, driven people, and the fact that you're here trying to work through it tells me something important about your resilience. I'm curious — when you think back before this exam, were there moments where you *did* feel like you belonged in your major, and what was different about those times?

client: I mean... yeah, there were moments, like when I did well on a project last semester and my professor actually praised my analysis in front of the class. But it feels almost impossible to hold onto that right now — it's like this one bad grade just erased all of that, and I can't quite trust that those good moments were real or that I actually earned them. I guess I'm not sure how looking back at the good times helps when this bad grade feels so much more true somehow.
therapist: What you're describing — where one painful experience feels more "true" than all the evidence pointing the other way — is actually a really well-recognized pattern our minds fall into, and it doesn't mean your brain is right, just that it's hurting right now. That professor didn't praise someone who didn't earn it, and that moment was just as real as this grade. I'm wondering, if a close friend came to you with exactly your situation — the praised analysis, the failed final — what would you tell them about whether they truly belonged?

client: I'd probably tell a friend that one bad grade doesn't erase everything else, that they clearly have ability if a professor singled them out like that. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it just... doesn't land the same way. It feels like I'm making excuses for myself, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily when maybe the failed exam is actually the honest truth about where I stand.
therapist: That gap you're noticing — where compassion flows easily toward a friend but feels like "making excuses" when directed at yourself — is such an important thing to catch, because it reveals a double standard you're holding yourself to that you wouldn't consider fair for anyone else. It's worth asking: why would the failed exam be the *honest* truth, but the professor's praise just luck or a fluke? What would it mean for you if both things were equally true — that you have real ability *and* that you struggled on this particular exam?

client: I guess... if both things were equally true, it would mean I'm not just one thing. Like, I can't keep hiding behind "I'm just bad at this" as a way to avoid the risk of actually trying and still failing. But honestly, that feels scarier than just accepting I'm not good enough, because then I'd have no excuse not to keep going, and what if I still mess up anyway?
therapist: You just said something really profound — that believing you're "not good enough" actually feels *safer* than believing in yourself, because it protects you from the risk of trying and still falling short. That's not weakness, that's a very human way of trying to avoid pain, but it's worth noticing that it's costing you something too. What do you think it would feel like to keep going *and* mess up sometimes — is that truly more unbearable than staying where you are right now?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, it kind of stops me in my tracks because I hadn't thought about it like that before. But I think messing up after actually trying would feel so much worse, because then I couldn't tell myself "well, I never really gave it a shot." Right now at least I have that excuse as a kind of... shield, I guess. I don't know if I'm ready to give that up.
therapist: The fact that you can see the shield so clearly right now — and name exactly what it's protecting you from — is actually a really meaningful step, because most people never get that far. You don't have to give it up all at once, and I'm not asking you to; but I want to gently reflect that the shield is also keeping out the experiences that might prove the critical voice wrong. What might one small, low-stakes way look like for you to test your ability — something where the cost of stumbling feels manageable rather than devastating?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually appreciates that you're not pushing me to just rip the shield away. But when you ask about "low-stakes" ways to test myself, my mind kind of goes blank, because honestly everything at work feels high-stakes to me — like even sending a simple email to my manager feels like it could go wrong and confirm everything I'm afraid of. I guess I'm not sure I trust my own ability to judge what's actually low-stakes versus what just looks low-stakes until it blows up in my face.
therapist: That feeling of everything being high-stakes is really exhausting, and it makes sense that your nervous system has gotten to a place where even small things carry the weight of the bigger fear underneath them. What if, instead of trying to find something that *feels* low-stakes right now, we got curious about what happens *after* one of those emails — like, how often does sending it actually confirm your worst fears versus just... being an email that got sent? I'm wondering if we might find that your fear radar is working overtime, and what the actual evidence of those smaller moments has been telling you?

client: I mean... I guess when I actually think about it, most of the emails just kind of disappear into the void, or I get a normal reply back. But it doesn't really feel that way in the moment — it still feels like every single one could be the one that makes someone think I'm incompetent or annoying. I don't know if tracking the evidence is going to change that gut feeling, even if my brain knows the numbers don't back up the fear.
therapist: You're touching on something really important — that knowing something logically and *feeling* it are two very different things, and CBT isn't about just thinking your way out of a feeling. But here's what I find meaningful: you just did something really significant by noticing that the evidence doesn't match the fear, even if your gut hasn't caught up yet, and that gap is actually where change slowly starts to happen. I'm curious — when you got one of those "normal replies" back, was there even a brief moment, however small, where you felt any relief or surprise that it went okay?

client: Yeah, I guess there was maybe a second or two where I thought "oh, okay, that wasn't as bad as I thought it would be." But then almost immediately my brain kind of jumped to "well, they're probably just being polite" or "they'll get tired of me eventually," and the relief just evaporated. It's like my mind won't let me hold onto the good part for more than a few seconds before it finds a way to cancel it out.
therapist: That pattern you're describing — where your mind almost immediately "cancels out" the relief — is actually the same thing that happened with your professor's praise, and it's worth noticing that this isn't random, it's your brain working very hard to protect that shield we talked about earlier. The good news is that you *are* having those moments of relief, however brief, which means some part of you is registering the evidence even if another part rushes in to erase it. What do you think it would take — even just a little — to let that "oh, that wasn't so bad" moment breathe for just a few seconds longer before your mind jumps in to cancel it?

client: I hear what you're saying, but honestly, letting that moment "breathe" feels almost dangerous, like if I stop bracing myself for the other shoe to drop, it'll hit me harder when it does. It's like my brain is convinced that the relief is a trap, and relaxing into it is just setting myself up for something worse. I don't know how to just... decide to trust it, even for a few seconds.
therapist: That image of relief feeling like a *trap* is so telling — your mind has essentially learned that staying braced and vigilant is how it keeps you safe, and it's been working hard at that job for a long time, so of course it doesn't want to stand down. But I want to gently point something out: you've been bracing for the other shoe to drop across all those emails, and by your own account, it mostly hasn't — which means the bracing may be costing you peace without actually protecting you from much. I'm wondering, can you think of a time in your life, even outside of work or school, where you let your guard down and it *didn't* end in the disaster you feared — what was that like?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there have been times. There was this one period a few years ago where I was waiting to hear back about a job application, and I just kind of gave up refreshing my email every five minutes and went out with a friend instead, and honestly the evening was fine, nothing catastrophic happened. But here's the thing — I still got rejected from that job eventually, so part of me feels like the vigilance was actually right, like the bad thing did come, I just wasn't watching for it when it did.
therapist: That's such a revealing example, because what it actually shows is that letting your guard down for an evening didn't *cause* the rejection or make it worse — the outcome was the same either way, but you got a good evening with a friend instead of hours of anxious refreshing. Your mind has quietly filed that story as "vigilance was right," but I'd gently offer another reading: the bad thing came regardless, and the only difference was whether you suffered *before* it arrived too. What would it mean for how you've been living if the vigilance has never actually been protecting you from outcomes, only from moments of peace?
